newsitem.title: USA: Fed issues transcripts of 1984 FOMC meetings.
newsitem.headline: Fed issues transcripts of 1984 FOMC meetings.

text.p: The Federal Reserve on Tuesday issued hundreds of pages of transcripts chronicling discussions that took place in 1984 during seven meetings of its policy setting Federal Open Market Committee that year.

Under pressure from Congress to make its operations more public, the Fed has begun periodically releasing complete transcripts of FOMC meetings that occurred at least five years ago. Briefer minutes of FOMC meetings are already released by the Fed 12 weeks after the meetings occur.

During 1984, the Fed first raised the discount rate one-half percentage point to nine percent early in April, breaking a string of nine declines that had begun in late 1981. Then it resumed lowering the discount rate, cutting it by half percentage points on Nov 21 and Dec 24 to end the year at 8 percent.

As the year began, then-Fed Chairman Paul Volcker was worried that the dollar was poised for a downturn, saying: "It seems to me that this would be a good time for us to begin stockpiling currencies to use if and when we get the kind of decline in the dollar that I feel is on the way."

During the year, as problems in the banking industry began to appear including a funding crisis for Continental Illinois bank, the dollar was buffeted and the Fed was forced to intervene to support it.

At the July 16-17 FOMC meeting, Volcker also worried that rising budget deficits were making it more difficult to craft monetary policy. "I won't berate the fact that we now have a financial system under pressure in every direction," Volcker said.
By October, then-Fed Governor Marth Seger was warning about a "terribly scary" potential for problems in the nation's savings and loan industry.

"I think a very large group will be going down the chute rather than a somewhat smaller group," Seger said. Later in the decade, primarily from 1988-91, hundreds of thrifts went bankrupt and a federal bailout was required.
Late in 1984, Volcker was still concerned about the dollar's movements, commenting at the Nov 7 meeting that he was willing to ease rates down a bit and be ready to defend the dollar if necessary.
"I would rather be in a position where, if anything, we have the easing done and are in a position to tighten up a little if the dollar does get in real trouble at some point," Volcker said.
